description: Hi! I'm Kexin, a graduate student in Computer Science at Wentworth Institute of Technology in Boston. I'm taking part in this challenge as a solo team. I'm interested in space history and storytelling. For the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge, I want to tell the stories of the equipment NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars, and show why these objects still matter today.
summary: Letters from the Moon and Mars is a free, kid-friendly web page where five machines that NASA left behind write letters to young space fans: the Apollo Moon buggies, the Apollo laser mirrors on the Moon, the Opportunity rover, the Ingenuity helicopter, and Voyager 1. Each letter tells, in simple English, where the machine is, what it did, what science it made possible, and how it is doing now. Fact cards, status badges and a short quiz connect the story to real NASA science. The project shows school-age students that "abandoned" hardware is not forgotten: some of it still works, and the rest left rocks, photos and data that scientists still use today.
details:
What it does: The page is written for students aged about 8 to 14. It starts with a simple "map" of three places (the Moon, Mars and deep space). Students pick a machine and read a letter written in its own voice. Below each letter there are fact cards with real numbers, a "Science I made possible" box, and a status badge that shows whether the machine still works or is retired. At the end, a four-question quiz gives instant feedback.

The five machines:

- Lunar Roving Vehicles (Apollo 15, 16, 17): the only cars ever driven on another world.

- Laser retroreflectors (Apollo 11, 14, 15): still used today to measure the Earth-Moon distance; they showed the Moon moves away about 3.8 cm per year.

- Opportunity rover: planned for 90 Martian days, worked almost 15 years, drove more than 45 km and found clues of ancient water.

- Ingenuity helicopter: the first aircraft to fly on another planet; 72 flights before a damaged rotor blade grounded it in January 2024.

- Voyager 1: launched in 1977, now in interstellar space and about one light-day from Earth in November 2026.

How it works: It is a single static web page built with HTML, CSS and a small amount of JavaScript (for the quiz). It works on phones, tablets and classroom projectors, needs no login, and is hosted for free on GitHub Pages.

Benefits and impact: Letters are short, personal and easy to read, so they turn technical facts into a story about a "friend" in space. The goal is to help kids see that space hardware has a life story, that some of it is still working, and that they could be the explorers who visit it one day.

Creativity: Instead of a list of facts, each machine speaks for itself. Status badges show at a glance which machines are still working, and the quiz turns reading into a game.

Future ideas: more letters (Spirit, Apollo lunar landers, Voyager 2), read-aloud audio for younger kids, and translations into Spanish and Chinese.

Tools used: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, GitHub Pages, and an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic). All AI-assisted illustrations are labeled on the page.
